messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mika, a 48-year-old married man of Pacific Islander background, had built his life around physical work and routine. As a roofer, he was used to early starts, long climbs, and the practical demands of a body that had to stay steady on ladders and uneven surfaces. Before the assault, he had been known as someone who kept going, someone who preferred hard work to talking about private matters. That changed after an incident that he still described carefully, as if naming it plainly might make it more bearable. He had been sexually assaulted by a man after drinking, and what lingered most for him was not only the violation itself but the combination of powerlessness, the smell of alcohol, and the sense that the night had been split in two, with everything afterward feeling altered.

In the weeks that followed, Mika found that reminders could arrive without warning and take hold immediately. If a news story mentioned sexual assault, even briefly, he would feel his attention lock onto it with a sick, involuntary intensity. He would keep watching or listening longer than he wanted to, unsettled by how quickly his body reacted, yet unable to turn away right away. Motorcycle noise was another sharp cue. When one passed too close on the street or rumbled by his worksite, the sound would cut through him in a way he found hard to explain, landing as a sudden jolt rather than an ordinary passing noise. At other times, the smell of alcohol was enough to make him tense and feel ill at ease, whether it came from a social gathering, a neighbor’s drink on a warm evening, or someone at a store. He came to plan around these moments, arranging his days so he would be less likely to encounter them, though life did not always cooperate.

Mika began to notice that memories of the assault did not sit in the past in the way other memories did. He described them as more real and more vivid than ordinary recollections, as though the event had been stamped into him with a force that everyday moments could not match. When the memory came, it was not always a full scene. Sometimes he was flooded with the emotional intensity first, a wave of dread and grief that arrived before any clear picture. At other times, a fragment would surface and pull everything with it. When he did remember it directly, he felt overwhelming grief, not only for what had happened but for what it seemed to have taken from him. He could still function, but the memory had a way of making him feel as though he were standing too close to something raw that had not finished happening.

Over time, Mika’s days narrowed. At work, he became increasingly careful about anything that put his body under stress. Roofing had always been strenuous, but now he found himself avoiding situations that left him feeling physically taxed more than necessary. He would push through the job, yet he planned his efforts more tightly, watching for opportunities to reduce strain when he could. At home, he tried to keep busy with other things. If there was an empty stretch of time, he filled it with errands, small tasks, or extra work. Stillness felt unsafe to him, not because he said so in dramatic terms, but because quiet left too much room for memory and feeling to arrive. He had also begun restricting his eating strictly, monitoring it as a way to feel in control of something in his life. The discipline gave him a brief sense of order, though it also made meals less relaxed and more governed by rules he seemed to impose on himself.

His wife had noticed that he was harder to reach emotionally, and his effort to stay occupied made him less available at home. He remained committed to work and to his marriage, but there was a sense that he was always managing himself in the background. He did not describe himself as falling apart. Instead, he described living with a constant need to stay one step ahead of whatever might catch him off guard. What finally brought him to seek help was that the reminders were becoming harder to contain, and the grief that arrived with them felt heavier than he could keep carrying alone. He came wanting relief from the intensity of the memories and from the way certain sounds, smells, and news stories could still take him over. More than anything, he hoped to feel like himself again without being ambushed by what had happened, and he was afraid that if he did nothing, his world would keep shrinking around the event that had already changed so much.
